event: Planned power reduction begins from 3200 MWt for turbine coastdown test; steady decrease initiated
physics_significance: Test was 4th attempt (1982 1983 1985 all failed); test specification called for 700-1000 MWt; power reduction by operators

event: Reactor power reduced to approximately 1600 MWt for test; grid dispatcher Kiev orders hold — test postponed
physics_significance: Power reduction began 12 hours before test; Kiev dispatcher needed Unit 4 power for daytime grid demand; 9-hour delay while maintaining partial power

event: ECCS (Emergency Core Cooling System) isolated per test procedure; NOT reconnected before accident
physics_significance: ECCS isolation was specified in test protocol; however it remained isolated for entire 9-hour delay and through accident; would not have prevented prompt criticality but removed emergency cooling fallback

event: Kiev dispatcher releases reactor; power reduction to test level resumes
physics_significance: After 9-hour hold; new shift begins; operators unfamiliar with current xenon condition; xenon-135 had been building up during hold at elevated power

event: Power drops to approximately 30 MWt (xenon pit); near-complete shutdown
physics_significance: Xenon-135 (t1/2=9.2h) built up to peak poisoning ~3000 pcm during 9-hour hold; when operators tried to reduce power they entered deep xenon pit; reactor nearly shut itself down; Xe-135 absorbs thermal neutrons → k_eff <<1

event: Operators withdraw most control rods to overcome xenon pit and stabilize power
physics_significance: To bring reactor out of xenon pit operators withdrew rods massively; this moved ORM from acceptable value toward minimum (15 rods); sets stage for catastrophically low ORM at test time; graphite tips now above core awaiting insertion

event: Power stabilized at approximately 200 MWt after xenon partial burnout over ~30 minutes
physics_significance: Xenon partially burned by neutron absorption during 200 MWt operation; reactor not stably controlled; shift foreman Aleksandr Akimov and supervisor Anatoly Dyatlov decided to proceed at 200 MWt despite being below test spec 700-1000 MWt

event: Two additional main circulation pumps started per test protocol; now 8 of 8 pumps running
physics_significance: Increased coolant flow was part of turbine rundown test; 8 pumps running at 200 MWt caused excessive core coolant flow → more subcooling → REDUCED void fraction → temporarily SUPPRESSED positive void coefficient; gave false impression of stability

event: Operators note increasing instability; coolant flow approaching limits
physics_significance: High coolant flow at low power created unstable thermal-hydraulic conditions; some operators concerned but Dyatlov pressed to continue; test had been delayed 9 hours

event: ORM measured at 8 rod-equivalents; below minimum required 15; shift foreman signed off
physics_significance: ORM = 8 rods = only 8 rod-equivalents of negative reactivity available for shutdown; minimum requirement was 15; post-accident minimum raised to 30; with ORM=8 nearly all control rods were withdrawn from active core; graphite displacer tips at top of core channels waiting to be inserted

event: Test begins: turbine steam supply valve closed; reactor now coast-down begins
physics_significance: With steam valve closed coolant flow to turbines stops; steam generator pressure increases; more boiling in core → INCREASING void fraction → INCREASING positive reactivity → power begins rising; the void coefficient feedback loop begins

event: Power >530 MWt and rapidly increasing; operator Leonid Toptunov initiates AZ-5 SCRAM
physics_significance: AZ-5 = full emergency shutdown button; all 211 control rods ordered to insert; but at ORM=8 nearly all rods were withdrawn with graphite displacer tips sitting ABOVE active core regions waiting to enter; SCRAM actually begins the excursion

event: Graphite displacer tips enter core during first 1-3 seconds of rod insertion; positive reactivity spike
physics_significance: Graphite tips (lower neutron absorption than water they displaced) add +2 to +3 beta positive reactivity as they enter the water-filled channels; this is the immediate cause of excursion; rods are physically moving toward shutdown but first make it worse

event: Reactor power excursion begins; power rising rapidly; fuel fragmentation begins at ~5x rated power (~16000 MWt)
physics_significance: Combined positive reactivity: graphite tips (+2-3β) + existing steam voids (~+7β) = total reactivity >>β (0.005); reactor went prompt critical; responds on prompt neutron lifetime ~10 microseconds; mechanical rods cannot stop it; power doubles every few milliseconds

event: First explosion: peak power estimated ~30000 MWt (10x rated); fuel fragmentation; steam explosion
physics_significance: Rapid fission power pulse → fuel temperature to ~3000°C (UO2 melts ~2850°C) → hot fuel fragments contact water → explosive steam generation; pressure wave destroys fuel channels; enormous pressure spike; 1000-tonne Elena reactor lid (biological shield) ejected vertically

event: Second explosion (disputed mechanism); 1000-tonne reactor lid ejected; reactor building roof destroyed
physics_significance: Second explosion hypothesis 1: steam (explosive steam release continuing); hypothesis 2: hydrogen from Zr+H2O → ZrO2+H2 ignition; hypothesis 3: small nuclear excursion (Pakhomov/Dubasov 2009); INSAG-7 (1991) revised INSAG-1 (1986): graphite tip effect = primary cause of first excursion; second explosion mechanism remains scientifically debated

event: Graphite fire begins; ~300 tonnes of ejected graphite burning on roof and surroundings; multiple roof fires
physics_significance: Graphite moderator blocks ejected at >1200°C catch fire on contact with air; extremely difficult to extinguish (graphite fire requires thermal smothering not water — water on burning graphite produces explosive H2); first firefighters called; 28 fire brigade personnel respond

event: First firefighters arrive from Chernobyl fire station; begin fighting building and roof fires
physics_significance: Firefighters not warned of radiation hazard; told it was 'ordinary fire'; standard firefighting gear only; many received fatal radiation doses fighting roof fires directly on highly contaminated graphite; 28 acute deaths from ARS

event: Firefighting continues; ~237 emergency workers examined; first ARS signs appear (nausea vomiting skin erythema)
physics_significance: Vomiting began within 1-4 hours in highest-dose recipients (Grade III-IV ARS); early vomiting is diagnostic of ARS grade; Dr. Angelina Guskova at Moscow Hospital No.6 begins establishing clinical protocol

event: Reactor fire and graphite fire declared extinguished by fire brigade; but graphite fire in reactor core continues
physics_significance: Surface fires extinguished; core graphite fire underground continued for 10 days; this is the source of continued radionuclide release April 26 - May 9

event: First radiation measurements: 1000-3600 R/hr (10-36 Sv/hr) at various locations near reactor
physics_significance: Soviet civil defense dosimeters saturated at 1000 R/hr (not calibrated for accident-level fields); true doses in some areas exceeded instrument range; measurements used for evacuation decisions

event: Valery Khodemchuk's body confirmed missing in reactor rubble (never recovered); Vladimir Shashenok pronounced dead from burns and radiation at Prypiat Hospital
physics_significance: First 2 confirmed deaths: Khodemchuk died in steam explosion; Shashenok died of combined thermal and radiation injuries; 28 more ARS deaths would follow

event: Soviet leadership informed; OPAS (special nuclear accident response) system activated; USSA committee sent to site
physics_significance: Information kept secret from public; no evacuation order yet; Prypiat residents (49000) not informed for 36 hours; Soviet system required ministerial approval for emergency actions

event: Helicopter survey of reactor; graphite and fuel scattered in wide area confirmed; aerial radiation measurements begin
physics_significance: Helicopter survey confirmed catastrophic core destruction; extent of contamination visible; decision made to begin aerial drops but logistics required time; high gamma fields deterred ground survey

event: Start of helicopter aerial drops: sand lead dolomite boron carbide to cover reactor and extinguish graphite fire
physics_significance: 1800 helicopter flights total; 2400t lead + 1800t sand/clay + 800t dolomite + 40t boron + other; boron to prevent criticality restart; materials mostly did not reach reactor core cavity effectively due to strong updraft of hot gas

event: Prypiat executive committee meets to discuss evacuation; Soviet Politburo contacted
physics_significance: 36-hour delay in Prypiat evacuation; residents continued normal activities including outdoors; children played in schoolyards April 26; high I-131 deposition occurring; irreversible thyroid dose accumulating especially in children

event: Evacuation of Prypiat (49000 people) officially ordered; preparation begins
physics_significance: Official order came 36+ hours post-accident; preparation required collecting 1100 buses from Kiev region; KI (potassium iodide) tablets NOT distributed in Prypiat before evacuation

event: Prypiat evacuation begins; residents told they could return in 3 days (they never did)
physics_significance: Evacuation completed in approximately 3.5 hours for 49000 people using 1100 buses; residents told temporary evacuation for 3 days; many left without taking personal documents; never permitted to return permanently

event: Forsmark Nuclear Power Plant (Sweden, 1100 km away) detects radiation on workers' clothing; identifies as Chernobyl isotope mix
physics_significance: Worker at Forsmark stepped on something on the ground and set off contamination alarms; shoes contained Chernobyl-origin particles; Swedish scientists identified I-131/Cs-134/Cs-137 ratio as reactor accident; forced first Soviet admission of accident

event: Soviet news agency TASS issues 14-word statement: 'An accident has occurred at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant; one of the reactors was damaged. Measures are being taken to eliminate the consequences.'
physics_significance: First (and minimal) official Soviet public acknowledgment; approximately 64 hours after explosion; no details about scale; no radiation monitoring advice to public; Western media had already been reporting from Swedish detection

event: Second plume path: Central and Southern Europe affected (Austria Germany Poland France)
physics_significance: Wind shift directed plume south and southwest; May 1 1986 plume reaches France; May 5 Magdeburg Germany thunderstorm deposits ~75000 Bq/kg Cs-137 on grass; Romanian mountains peak 176 mBq/m3 Cs-137 in air

event: Poland becomes ONLY country in USSR/Eastern Bloc to distribute KI tablets; 18 million people receive tablets
physics_significance: Polish health authorities acted independently and early; KI blocks thyroid uptake of I-131 when given within 2h of exposure; Polish thyroid cancer rates dramatically lower than Belarus/Ukraine despite similar deposition levels in eastern Poland

event: 30-km exclusion zone formally established; 135000 people ordered to evacuate from surrounding villages
physics_significance: Initial 10km zone expanded to 30km zone; villages within zone evacuated over following days; total 115000-135000 people displaced; many received significant doses during the days before evacuation

event: Third plume path reaches UK and Ireland; May 1-10 1986
physics_significance: Plume reaches British Isles; UK maximum milk I-131 12-77 Bq/L depending on region; Ireland maximum milk 441 Bq/L; restrictions on sheep (North Wales/Cumbria UK) lasted for years; Met Eireann confirmed arrival via rain events

event: Soviet decision to flood tunnel under reactor foundation to install cooling system (China Syndrome concern)
physics_significance: Fear that corium could melt through foundation and contaminate groundwater (China Syndrome); 400 workers dug tunnel in 15 days; heat exchanger installed; ultimately unnecessary — corium solidified naturally; workers received significant doses

event: Graphite fire in reactor core declared extinguished after 13 days
physics_significance: Graphite fire burned from April 26 to May 9; was primary driver of high-altitude radionuclide release to European plume; aerial drops of 5000 tonnes finally effective with sand/clay physical smothering; fire extinguished by May 9 per OECD-NEA Ch.II

event: Soviet leader Gorbachev makes first TV address about accident; 18 days post-accident
physics_significance: First major public Soviet acknowledgment of scale of disaster; partial information only; international relations with IAEA; led to eventual greater transparency compared to initial coverup

event: Liquidator campaigns: 600000-800000 workers from USSR mobilized for cleanup operations
physics_significance: Liquidators included firefighters military personnel miners civil workers scientists; tasks included roof cleanup (highly radioactive graphite), decontamination of buildings, soil removal, construction; doses varied enormously: highest doses in 1986 roof cleaners

event: Roof decontamination begins; 'bio-robots' (humans in lead shielding) remove graphite from roof by hand
physics_significance: Called 'bio-robots' because real robots failed (electronics failed in radiation fields); workers given only 90 seconds on the roof; many received 25-35 rem per 90 seconds shift; over 3000 workers cleaned the roof; all received significant doses

event: Original concrete 'sarcophagus' (Object Shelter) construction completed; encases destroyed reactor
physics_significance: Sarcophagus built in 206 days by ~90000 construction workers; not airtight; designed for 30-year lifetime; contains 170-220 tonnes corium; ~1375 m3 of radioactive water accumulated inside

event: Trial of six Chernobyl plant officials begins; Dyatlov Bryukhanov Fomin and 3 others convicted
physics_significance: Anatoly Dyatlov (deputy chief engineer who supervised test) received 10 years; Viktor Bryukhanov (plant director) 10 years; all charges related to violations of safety procedures; reactor design flaws NOT acknowledged in 1987 trial; INSAG-7 (1991) later revised root cause attribution

event: INSAG-7 published; revises INSAG-1 (1986) root cause; identifies both design flaws AND operator violations as necessary causes
physics_significance: INSAG-1 (1986) blamed primarily operators; INSAG-7 (1991) acknowledged graphite tip effect and positive void coefficient as essential contributors; 'neither the design deficiencies nor the operators' procedural violations alone would have been sufficient to cause the accident'

event: Chernobyl Unit 3 (last operating unit) shut down; all Chernobyl units now permanently closed
physics_significance: Units 1-3 continued operating after accident (Unit 2 shut 1991 after fire; Unit 1 shut 1996; Unit 3 shut Dec 15 2000); final shutdown under international pressure and Ukrainian government decision; ISF-2 dry cask storage project begins

event: New Safe Confinement (NSC) successfully slid over old sarcophagus; largest moveable land structure ever built
physics_significance: NSC: 108m high; 162m wide; 257m long; arch steel structure; 36000 tonnes; built 300m away then slid on teflon rails over sarcophagus in 2-week operation; designed for 100-year lifetime; prevents further radionuclide release from deteriorating sarcophagus

event: Russian military forces seize Chernobyl site during invasion of Ukraine; heavy vehicle traffic in Red Forest
physics_significance: Russian military convoy passed through Red Forest (most contaminated soil in CEZ); tracked vehicles resuspended contaminated soil particles; dose rates spiked to 70x normal for ~2 days; IAEA lost continuous monitoring contact; trench-digging in Red Forest area documented

event: Russian forces withdraw from Chernobyl site; Ukrainian authorities re-establish control
physics_significance: Continuous IAEA remote monitoring restored; dose rates returned to pre-invasion levels after ~48 hours of elevated readings; vegetation regrowth in disturbed areas began; some contamination redistribution from vehicle disturbance; ongoing assessment

event: New Safe Confinement sustains damage from drone strike; structural assessment and repair planning initiated
physics_significance: Drone strike caused assessed damage to NSC structure; IAEA confirmed no significant radiological release during incident; structural integrity maintained but repairs required; Sep 2025 repair work planned

event: Mirion Technologies OSL integrated monitoring system installed within NSC; radiation measurements improved
physics_significance: New optically stimulated luminescence dosimetry system provides better spatial dose mapping inside NSC; improves monitoring of corium regions and spent fuel areas

event: NSC experiences 16-hour power loss; backup systems activated; no radiological release confirmed
physics_significance: Grid power loss to NSC electrical systems; ventilation and monitoring ran on backup power; 16-hour event resolved; ongoing war-related grid instability in Ukraine is persistent risk factor for Chernobyl site

event: 40th anniversary of Chernobyl accident; current dose rates (SaveEcoBot): Prypiat 4.932 µSv/h; Chornobyl city 0.209 µSv/h
physics_significance: Current Prypiat dose rate ~4.932 µSv/h = ~43 mSv/yr; above 1 mSv/yr public dose limit; town remains uninhabitable; Chornobyl city 0.209 µSv/h ≈ 1.8 mSv/yr; near background; some return possible; Am-241 still increasing toward 2058.7 peak
